vocab.notes: ze before some consonant groups: ze Skotska, ze Slovenska.
A soft feminine noun: the genitive looks the same as the nominative.
Česko (Czechia) is the everyday short name: Bydlím v Česku. Česká republika (the Czech Republic) is the formal one, on forms and in the news: z České republiky. You'll hear both.
Bydlím v Praze. I live in Prague.
Literally "What are you doing?", but also used to ask about someone's job.

dialogue.setting: Drinks after work for a colleague's birthday. Sam, who has just moved to Prague from England, meets Petra.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.cs: Jsem z [[Anglie|Anglie|gen|after-z]], z [[Manchesteru|Manchester|gen|after-z]]. A ty? Jsi z [[Prahy|Praha|gen|after-z]]?
lines.en: I'm from England, from Manchester. And you? Are you from Prague?

lines.speaker: Petra
lines.cs: Ne, jsem z [[Brna|Brno|gen|after-z]], ale bydlím v [[Praze|Praha|loc|location-v-na]].
lines.en: No, I'm from Brno, but I live in Prague.

lines.speaker: Petra
lines.en: I'm a teacher. I teach English. And you?

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.en: I'm a programmer. I work from home.

hints.explain: America would be "z Ameriky". He says "z Anglie": from England.
From Prague would be "z Prahy". He says "z Anglie, z Manchesteru".

exercises.why: "Jsem z Anglie, z Manchesteru." I'm from England, from Manchester. z + genitive: Anglie, Manchesteru.

exercises.listen: Ne, jsem z Brna, ale bydlím v Praze.
options: In Prague, but she's from Brno
answers: In Prague, but she's from Brno

hints.explain: She's from Brno ("z Brna") but lives in Prague ("bydlím v Praze").
No mention of England here: "bydlím v Praze", I live in Prague.

exercises.why: "Ne, jsem z Brna, ale bydlím v Praze." No, I'm from Brno, but I live in Prague.
z (from) takes the genitive. Feminine nouns in -a change it to -y: Kanada → z Kanady, Praha → z Prahy.

hints.explain: Kanada is the nominative (dictionary form). After z, use the genitive: z Kanady.

exercises.why: z takes the genitive. Neuter nouns in -o change it to -a: Brno → z Brna.

hints.explain: Brno is the nominative. After z, use the genitive: z Brna.

exercises.why: Anglie is a soft feminine noun (like růže). Its genitive singular looks the same as the nominative: z Anglie.

hints.explain: -y is for nouns ending in -a (Kanada → z Kanady). Anglie ends in -e, and its genitive stays z Anglie.

exercises.question: Which case is "Prahy"?
exercises.why: After z (from), Czech always uses the genitive: Praha → z Prahy.
odkud means "from where": Odkud jsi? (formal: Odkud jste?)

hints.explain: Kde jsi? means "Where are you (right now)?". For where someone comes from, use odkud: Odkud jsi?
Odkud jste? is the formal (vy) form. Informal: Odkud jsi?

exercises.why: Words for jobs and nationalities have masculine and feminine forms: učitel / učitelka. Czech has no word for "a".

hints.explain: učitel is the masculine form. A woman says: Jsem učitelka.

exercises.prompt: I live in Prague, but I'm from Brno.
answers: Bydlím v Praze, ale {jsem|pocházím} z Brna.
exercises.why: Use v + locative for where you live (v Praze) and z + genitive for where you're from (z Brna).

hints.wrong: Bydlím v Praze, ale {jsem|pocházím} z Brno.
hints.explain: After z (from), use the genitive: Brno → z Brna.

hints.wrong: Bydlím v Praha, ale {jsem|pocházím} z Brna.
hints.explain: After v (in), the noun changes too: Praha → v Praze. You'll practise this in unit 3.

exercises.why: Verbs in -ovat change -ova- to -uj-: pracuju (or pracuji), pracuješ, pracuje, pracujeme, pracujete, pracujou.

hints.explain: Verbs in -ovat don't keep -ova- in the present: pracovat → pracuju.
pracuje is the on/ona form. For já: pracuju.
